ann_34.text: Through this part, chest pain brought on by exercise clearly raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 78%, an abnormal thallium result clearly raises it to about 56%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute clearly lowers it from about 39% to about 22%.
Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises it to about 90%, a flat ST segment to about 69%, and higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 17% to about 47% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 1%, typical angina and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 5%, and non-anginal chest pain to about 7% (on the training data only).
Atypical angina raises it here from about 28% to about 39%, older age (42 to 66 years) from about 22% to about 32%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 33% (on the training data only).
A downsloping ST segment slightly lowers it, from about 28% to about 25% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 17 patients).

ann_35.text: This part acts on 135 of 242 training patients (56%); 81 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, 1.5 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 90% to about 94% (on the training data only).
Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 24% to about 52%, and only once it rises above about 0.4 mm (on the training data only).

ann_36.text: This part acts on 148 of 242 training patients (61%); 70 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 57-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a resting blood pressure of 140 mm Hg, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy and a normal thallium scan), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 35% to about 37% (on the training data only).

Through it, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) slightly raises a typical patient's predicted risk, from about 27% to about 31%, and only once it rises above about 128 mm Hg (on the training data only).

ann_37.text: This part acts on 112 of 242 training patients (46%); 63 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 55-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, a maximum heart rate of 158 beats per minute, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, an upsloping ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it raises the predicted risk from about 42% to about 55% (on the training data only).
Through it, a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute raises that patient's predicted risk from about 46% to about 55% (on the training data only).

Resting blood pressure adds to the predicted risk here only once it rises above about 111 mm Hg (for the typical patient with a fold, from about 85% to about 90%), and for a typical patient only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_38.text: This part acts on 79 of 242 training patients (33%); 44 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 54-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, chest pain brought on by exercise, a resting blood pressure of 125 mm Hg, an upsloping ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 65% to about 34% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina clearly lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 5%.

Chest pain brought on by exercise lowers it here from about 28% to about 16%, and for the typical patient it acts on, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) raises it from about 23% to about 61% (on the training data only).
Higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain (from about 9% to about 65%, against about 26% to about 31% without it).
It also raises it more with atypical angina (from about 4% to about 18%, against about 26% to about 31%) (on the training data only).

ann_39.text: This part acts on 102 of 242 training patients (42%), patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less; 59 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 55-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms, chest pain brought on by exercise, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy, a flat ST segment and a reversible defect on the thallium scan), it lowers the predicted risk from about 99% to about 81% (on the training data only).
Through it, atypical angina clearly lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 5%.

For the typical patient it acts on, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL, being a woman or a downsloping ST segment raise the predicted risk from about 81% to about 99%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 76% to about 85% (on the training data only; the model has little data on the downsloping ST segment, 17 patients).

Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL and being a woman clearly lower the predicted risk more if exercise does not bring on chest pain (from about 28% to about 5% and to about 1%) than if it does (from about 26% to about 33% and to about 12%).

Atypical angina and a fixed thallium defect lower the predicted risk when fasting blood sugar is 120 mg/dL or less (from about 28% to about 9% and to about 6%), but the other way when it is higher (from about 5% to about 8% and to about 15%). The model has little data on this: only 15 training patients (a fixed defect on the thallium scan).

ann_40.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 5%) or non-anginal chest pain (about 7%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 28%).
A maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute clearly lowers a typical patient's predicted risk, from about 39% to about 22%.
Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises it to about 90%, a flat ST segment to about 69%, and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 54% (on the training data only).

Higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) raises it from about 17% to about 47%, more ST depression (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 24% to about 52%, older age (42 to 66 years) from about 22% to about 32%, higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 26% to about 31%, and signs of left ventricular hypertrophy to about 33% (on the training data only).
Being a woman lowers it to about 1% (on the training data only).
A thallium result coded 4 raises it to about 56% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, 2 patients).

ann_34.original: Direct input-to-output edges: a 15-input linear logit. Largest weights (per train SD): ca +1.42, exang:1 +1.06, sex:1 +0.95 (with sex:0 -0.59, i.e. +3.25 logit male vs female), slope:2 +0.94, cp:3 -0.75, fbs:1 -0.67, chol +0.61, thal:3 -0.59, cp:1 -0.58, thalach -0.32, age +0.20, cp:2 +0.20, restecg:2 +0.12, slope:1 +0.06. Evidence: closed form exact (linear). Train SD of this term 3.88 logit, AUC alone 0.910; mean-ablating it drops model AUC 0.954 -> 0.508, so it is the backbone. It double-counts male sex and exercise angina, which protective_gate corrects.
ann_34.proposed: An additive part: chest pain on exercise, an abnormal thallium result, more vessels, a flat ST segment, higher cholesterol, atypical angina, older age and left ventricular hypertrophy raise the predicted risk; a higher maximum heart rate, being a woman, typical or non-anginal chest pain and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lower it.

ann_35.original: ReLU hinge on ST depression: 8065 = relu(1.25 oldpeak + 0.629), read out +0.483. Zero for oldpeak below -0.50 SD (the many patients with oldpeak 0 sit around -0.87, so this is 'any ST depression'), then +0.60 logit per SD. Evidence: closed form exact; train line plot over 242 points, active for 56% of patients, correlation 0.99 with oldpeak. Contribution SD 0.54 logit; mean-ablating it drops AUC 0.954 -> 0.947. Only route by which oldpeak reaches the output.
ann_35.proposed: ST depression above about 0.4 mm raises the predicted risk.

ann_36.original: ReLU hinge on resting blood pressure: 8900 = relu(0.957 trestbps + 0.241), read out +0.138, i.e. +0.13 logit per SD above trestbps -0.25 SD. Evidence: closed form exact; train line plot (242 points, active 61%). Contribution SD only 0.10 logit; mean-ablating it changes AUC by <0.001. Near-inert; the meaningful blood-pressure effect runs through protective_gate.
ann_36.proposed: Resting blood pressure above about 128 mm Hg slightly raises the predicted risk.

ann_37.original: 1754 = relu(0.914 relu(trestbps + 0.5 thalach + 1.17) - 0.013): two stacked ReLUs that act as an almost linear ramp in resting BP plus half max heart rate (corr 0.98 with trestbps+0.5 thalach; floor at 0 for 16% of patients with very low BP/HR). Feeds protective_gate with weight -0.30, so higher BP/HR closes the gate. Evidence: closed form exact; train sensitivity |d1754/d trestbps| 0.76, |d/d thalach| 0.38 (ratio 2:1 as the weights imply).
ann_37.proposed: A part through which resting blood pressure above about 111 mm Hg and a higher maximum heart rate raise the predicted risk of the patients it acts on.

ann_38.original: Serial chain on exercise angina, resting BP and cp:2. 7659 = relu(1.04 exang:1 - 1.31) is a constant flag (0.153 for angina patients, 0 otherwise). 6931 = relu(0.945 exang:1 - 0.629 trestbps + 0.955*7659 + 0.31): for angina patients about 1.78 - 0.63 trestbps (active 99%), for others only when BP is low (32%). 4652 = relu(1.02*6931 + 1.17 cp:2 - 0.30): large for cp:2 (mean 2.51, always active) and for angina with low BP. So the exit encodes 'angina or non-anginal chest pain (cp:2), the more so the lower the resting BP'. Feeds protective_gate with +0.63. Evidence: closed form exact; train sensitivity exang 0.67, cp:2 0.55, trestbps 0.23.
ann_38.proposed: A part through which atypical angina and chest pain on exercise lower the predicted risk, and higher resting blood pressure raises it, more so with chest pain on exercise.

ann_39.original: Composition (parallel children feeding one ReLU): 2065 = relu(-0.618 + 0.847 sex:1 - 1.26 fbs:1 + 0.483 exang:1 - 0.473 slope:3 + 0.51 thal:6 + 0.136 thal:7 + 0.625 angina_bp_chain - 0.299 bp_hr_ramp), read out -1.63 into the logit. Hypothesis: a sub-additivity correction for the linear score's male and angina terms. It opens for men (60% open vs 7% of women), angina patients (71% vs 28%), cp:2 men (88%), thal:6/thal:7; fasting sugar fbs:1 closes it completely (0 of 33 open); higher resting BP/HR (via both children) narrows it. When open it subtracts 1.63*2065 (mean 2.3 logit among the 42% open). Evidence (train, 242 rows, counterfactual flips through the full model): male-vs-female effect +3.06 logit without angina but +1.36 with angina (linear part alone +3.25); angina effect +1.61 for women but +0.06 for men (linear part +2.23); cp:2 effect -1.48 in men vs -0.27 in women; d logit/d trestbps +0.81 per SD in gate-open patients vs +0.10 in closed. So: male sex and exercise angina are each strong risk signals but do not add up, and among such patients cp:2 chest pain and low BP mark lower risk. Mean-ablating the gate drops train AUC 0.954 -> 0.920 and raises log-loss 0.281 -> 0.379; within the open subgroup AUC 0.949 vs 0.903 without the gate. Sensitivity of 2065: fbs:1 0.53, sex:1 0.36, 4652 0.26, thal:6 0.21, exang 0.20, slope:3 0.20, 1754 0.13, thal:7 0.06. Caveat: slope:3 and thal:6 terms rest on 17 and 15 patients.
ann_39.proposed: A part acting on patients with fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less that lowers their predicted risk; through it atypical angina and chest pain on exercise lower the risk, and being a woman and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lower it more without chest pain on exercise.

ann_40.original: Root: P(disease) = sigmoid(0.228 + linear_score - 1.63*protective_gate + 0.483*oldpeak_hinge + 0.138*bp_hinge). Additive in the logit: a 15-input linear core (SD 3.88) plus one nonlinear interaction block (gate, SD 1.55) and two single-feature hinges (oldpeak SD 0.54, BP SD 0.10). Six inputs (cp:4, fbs:0, restecg:0, restecg:1, exang:0, thal:4) are unconnected and have zero effect (their one-hot partners carry the information). Evidence (train, 242 rows): train AUC 0.954 (acc 0.884); mean-ablation AUC: linear 0.508, gate 0.920, oldpeak 0.947, BP hinge 0.953, all nonlinear terms 0.910. Root sensitivity (prob scale): gate 0.154, linear 0.095, oldpeak 0.046, BP 0.013, unconnected 0. Full-model KernelSHAP (train, all 242 rows, prob scale) mean |SHAP|: ca 0.136, slope:2 0.106, cp:3 0.071, thal:3 0.068, sex:0 0.057, sex:1 0.049, chol 0.048, oldpeak 0.045, cp:1 0.038, exang:1 0.036, trestbps 0.033, cp:2 0.033, thal:6 0.027, fbs:1 0.023, thalach 0.021; unconnected inputs ~0.001 (sampling noise).
ann_40.proposed: Typical angina, non-anginal chest pain, being a woman and a higher maximum heart rate lower the predicted risk; more vessels, a flat ST segment, a reversible thallium defect, higher cholesterol, more ST depression, older age, higher resting blood pressure and left ventricular hypertrophy raise it.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk of heart disease about 28%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk with typical angina (about 5%) or non-anginal chest pain (about 7%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises a typical patient's predicted risk to about 90%, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment to about 69%, a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 54%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 17% to about 47%, and more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) from about 24% to about 52% (on the training data only).

Being a woman clearly lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: from about 28% to about 1% without chest pain on exercise, and from about 26% to about 12% with it.
A maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute clearly lowers a typical patient's predicted risk, from about 39% to about 22%.

Higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: from about 9% to about 65% with chest pain on exercise, and from about 26% to about 31% without it.

Fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL clearly lowers the predicted risk, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: from about 28% to about 5% without chest pain on exercise, against about 26% to about 33% with it.

confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points

summary.text: For a typical patient, number of vessels coloured by fluoroscopy going from 0 vessels to 2 vessels raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 28% to about 90% (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the ST segment is flat at peak exercise (about 69%) than if the ST segment slopes up at peak exercise (about 28%) (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, serum cholesterol going from 193 mg/dL (5.0 mmol/L) to 308 mg/dL (8.0 mmol/L) raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 17% to about 47% (on the training data only).

A higher resting blood pressure clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if exercise brings on chest pain: for a typical patient, resting blood pressure going from 110 mm Hg to 155 mm Hg moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 9% to about 65% if exercise brings on chest pain, and from about 26% to about 31% if exercise does not bring on chest pain.

Through one part of the model, ST depression on exercise only adds to the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 0.4 mm: for a typical such patient, going from 0.0 mm to 3.5 mm moves it from about 24% to about 61% (on the training data only).
